issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Faris Haddad is a 40-year-old paramedic who came to treatment nearly a year after the call that changed how he understood himself. He had been working a weekend shift when dispatch sent his unit to a highway collision involving a family sedan and a delivery truck. When he reached the scene, he recognized the passenger before he fully registered the wreckage: his younger sister's husband had been driving, and his sister Layla was in the back seat beside their injured son. There was blood across Layla's face and neck, glass in her hair, and the chemical smell of fuel mixed with the sharp antiseptic odor from the trauma supplies he tore open with shaking hands. He remembers flashes with terrible clarity-the wet shine of an open wound, Layla looking at him and saying his name, his nephew crying-and other parts are missing altogether. He cannot piece together exactly when he moved from the truck to the car, or the sequence of what he said. What does return comes back with the same terror he felt there, not as a story but as something happening again in full sensory detail.

In the weeks afterward, Faris had come to believe that this memory proved something devastating about him. He was certain he had failed in the one situation in which being a paramedic and a brother should have meant he could protect his family. The blank spots in his memory tormented him; because he could not account for everything he had done, he took the gaps as evidence that he could not rely on himself when it mattered most. Each reliving left him feeling permanently altered, as if the competent version of himself had been replaced by someone weaker and less dependable. Those conclusions sharpened what caught his attention. On shift, visible injuries on patients no longer looked like routine parts of the job but like accusations, and even passing the ambulance bay sink when it smelled of antiseptic could make his body brace before he had consciously placed why.

Those reminders quickly began pulling him back into the crash. A scalp laceration on a patient, a child mentioning his mother, the hospital-clean smell in an emergency department could make the scene with Layla surge up as fully real, with the same sensory force and panic. At work he would lose track of report details midway through listening, because his concentration narrowed around the feeling that something awful was about to happen again. He startled violently if a colleague touched his shoulder from behind, and in break rooms or waiting areas he automatically chose the chair with the clearest view of the door and the most protected position against the wall. As he became more keyed up, he noticed more reminders everywhere: every wound looked too much like that night, every victim's face risked turning into his sister's, every medicinal smell seemed to announce another disaster.

Faris responded by trying not to think about the crash at all. He would clamp down on images, push away Layla's voice, and tell himself to stay focused on tasks. On days off he found excuses to pick up errands or projects around the house simply to keep his mind occupied, and when he could not avoid work altogether he overworked within it-restocking excessively, volunteering for extra administrative tasks, burying himself in checklists. Yet the harder he fought the memory, the more abruptly it returned. Suppressing it seemed to make the missing pieces feel even more ominous, and his frantic busyness left him more brittle, more easily startled, and more likely to scan for the next reminder. He began dreading shifts because he knew they exposed him to injured bodies and victim stories, but staying away from work also fed his fear that he was no longer the kind of man who could do his job.

At home, the pattern tightened further. When his wife touched him unexpectedly while he was distracted, he jerked away in alarm and then felt ashamed. That reaction confirmed, in his mind, that he had changed for the worse. The shame pushed him to withdraw into chores or extra shifts rather than talk, and the distance this created in his marriage became one more sign that he was failing people he loved. His constant need to sit facing entrances in restaurants or family gatherings embarrassed him, but he felt he had to stay prepared. Living that way kept him on edge, and being on edge made the crash easier to relive and the triggers easier to spot.

He finally sought help after freezing during a pediatric trauma call when the antiseptic smell and the sight of facial injuries brought Layla's bloodied face back so completely that for a moment he was no longer sure where he was. He finished the call, but afterward he sat in the ambulance unable to concentrate, convinced he could not trust himself and terrified that next time someone would suffer because of him. What he wants most is to be able to go to work, come home to his wife, and remember that night without being dropped back into it; what he fears most is that the man who failed to protect his family is now the only version of him left.
